title: One decade a day
hook: a whole rosary takes about twenty minutes; a single decade is a real prayer too

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Salve Regina, the old prayer that closes the rosary. Your line was our life, our sweetness, our hope. Did you name a hard thing, and then a hope? Day one hundred twenty-four.

Meant to pray the rosary. Didn't. Plenty of people with beads in a drawer could say that. A whole rosary, five decades with the opening and closing prayers, takes about twenty minutes. That's a long time on a Tuesday with a sick kid and an inbox. So it slides. And then it slides for a month. And the beads sit in a drawer looking at you. Today's lesson is small on purpose. It's about what happens if, instead of twenty minutes, you give it four. One decade a day.
screen: `TWENTY MINUTES ON A TUESDAY.` → `THE BEADS IN THE DRAWER.` → `WHAT IF IT WERE FOUR?`

segments.voice: Start with the word bead. In Old English, the word gebed meant a prayer. People counted prayers on strings of small balls, and over time the name of the prayer slid over onto the thing you counted it on. A bead was a prayer before it was a bead. Now the decade: one Our Father, ten Hail Marys, one Glory Be, with one mystery held in mind. Said at a normal pace it takes three or four minutes. Is that a real prayer, or a cut-down one? The rosary isn't a single block that only counts if you finish it. It's built from decades, and each one stands on its own, with its own beginning and end: an Our Father, the Hail Marys, a Glory Be. Some Catholics pray a decade on the drive to work, walking the dog, or waiting for the kettle. Some carry a single decade ring or a small one-decade chaplet in a pocket. The arithmetic is simple. Seven decades in a week is more than one whole rosary. And a decade fits inside a Tuesday. That's our whole week on the rosary: how it's built, the joyful, luminous, sorrowful and glorious mysteries, the Salve Regina, and now this. Ten beads is enough to begin.
screen: `A BEAD WAS A PRAYER.` · `ONE DECADE: THREE OR FOUR MINUTES.` · `EACH DECADE STANDS ON ITS OWN.` · `SEVEN DECADES, MORE THAN ONE ROSARY.` · then, large: `TEN BEADS IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a decade you can take on a walk. Right now, let's just learn the feel of ten. Settle, and breathe. Rest one hand open. With each slow breath, fold down one finger. Ten breaths, ten fingers. If you pray the rosary, you can say a Hail Mary on each one instead, with one mystery in mind. If you don't, just count the breaths and notice how short ten really is. Later today, try it on a walk, one decade between here and the corner. The bell holds the time.
Decade. One Our Father, ten Hail Marys and a Glory Be, said in three or four minutes, a real prayer on its own. Today's word.

Your line: ten beads is enough. Today, find four minutes you'd have wasted anyway, in a line or on a walk, and give them one decade or ten slow breaths. Tomorrow we begin the seven sacraments. Day one hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Some Catholics who can't pray a full rosary pray a single decade each day, often while walking, driving or waiting, sometimes on a one-decade ring or pocket chaplet.

options: wait for a free twenty minutes.

put the beads away for good.
fork.reveal: one decade is a whole prayer, with its own beginning and end. seven in a week is more than one rosary.

original.note: Old English: a prayer. It gave us the word bead, the thing prayers were counted on.

trapdoor: what you thought: one decade is a shortcut, a rosary for people who can't be bothered.
what it means: each decade is a whole prayer, with its own beginning and end, small enough for any day.
what a scholar hears: bead comes from Old English gebed, prayer; the counted prayer lent its name to the counter.

notes: Timing: about twenty minutes for five decades, three to four minutes per decade; an estimate. Confirm.
Etymology of 'bead' from Old English gebed (prayer) via Middle English bede: standard dictionary etymology. Confirm.
'Popes, parish priests and grandmothers have all recommended a decade a day' is a general claim; no specific papal citation given. Confirm or soften.
Decade rings and one-decade chaplets (e.g. Irish penal rosary) mentioned generally.
Carry and review close the rosary part (days 118–124); Fatima prayer after each decade, common in many places, not mentioned. Confirm whether to add.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer puts a confession in 'lots of Catholics'' mouths; cut the unsourced 'popes, parish priests and grandmothers have all recommended', 'Catholic teaching and practice say', 'many Catholics', and the uplift about small habits shaping a life and decades 'growing'. Day 118's duplicate bead/gebed etymology was removed there so this day keeps it.
